subtype: Approach: step away with support and a safe exit plan [Revision]
passage: In a rented room in Leeds, Siddiq read the message again: "Come alone tomorrow, the leader wants a private word." His stomach tightened. For weeks the evening meetings had felt friendly, but the private talks had begun asking for his passport "for safekeeping". He called Valentina, a friend from his course. "I want to stop going. Will you be at my flat at six?" She said yes and told him to ring his parents as well. The next day he did not go. Two members waited outside his building, and Valentina and a flatmate stayed at his side until they left. He wrote to the group that he would not be back and saved every message. His parents told him that if anyone threatened him he should call the police.

qa.q: What had the private talks begun asking for?
qa.a: The private talks had begun asking for his passport for safekeeping.

qa.q: How was Siddiq feeling when he read the message?
qa.a: Siddiq felt uneasy and anxious, and his stomach tightened.

qa.q: What else could Siddiq do, and why?
qa.a: Siddiq could tell a course tutor or the university welfare team and go to the police if threats came, because more people who know make the exit safer.

qa.q: How might Valentina have seen the situation?
qa.a: Valentina was probably worried but glad to be trusted, and ready to stay by his side.

grounding: Illustrates stepping away from a group by telling a trusted friend, avoiding private meetings and leaning on family with the police as a fallback.
